objective: Hold the site's pages to the ADR register, as the Markdown corpus already is. Thirteen pages carry a hundred and ninety citations and WP-100's guard reads none of them, which #313 raised as the more public half of the corpus: a design misstates an ADR to five people, a landing page misstates it to a review seat, a broker or a prospective tenant.
completed: tests/test_html_adr_citations.py holds thirteen pages to the register: 190 citations, 2 set claims, 3 count claims.
Every citation has a register row, and all five claims agree with it. No disagreement was found and no page's content is changed.
The pages' grammar is recorded rather than assumed, as #313 asked: aggregate claims by range and by count, never one status per identifier.
Two readings that are not claims are excluded by construction and documented: an entry criterion's required future state, and a design's status rather than an ADR's.
Seven controls, six isolated and one declared not.
tests/test_adr_citations.py gains a pointer to its sibling, so a reader of either finds the other.
remaining: Two-axis review of the head commit, then merge.
After merge: the two findings are reported on #313, which the operator or a later package closes.
observations: The ticket's instruction to read the pages before writing the reader was the whole of the work. A reader built on the Markdown grammar would have found five claims where it expected a hundred and ninety, and would have reported two defects that are not there: phases/p0.html's 'The ADRs P0 builds on are accepted ... accepted per the register, not DRAFT_REQUIRED' is an ENTRY CRITERION under a heading that says so, naming the current status as the thing that must change - the most careful phrasing on the site - and the same page's thirteen '(design, IN_REVIEW)' strings are a design's status, not an ADR's.

The first count reader matched fourteen phrases of which three were real, because it read 'accepted', 'proposed' and 'rejected' as statuses when they were ordinary English, and 'one's current row' as the number one. Requiring the register's own SCREAMING_CASE cut it to exactly the three genuine claims. The same lesson as WP-105's rejected widening: a reader that manufactures claims is worse than one that reads fewer.

The ticket asked whether pages repeat statuses freely, and whether the answer might be a rule rather than a test. They do not: five aggregate claims across a hundred and ninety citations, and the pages otherwise cite an identifier and link the register. A rule forbidding it is not needed, and that is reported on #313.

One genuine tension found and reported rather than changed: landing/architecture.html states its counts 'by this page's count of the table', and SHOWCASE-001 says a count on a page is copied from the record it cites, never computed on the page. The page is transparent about it and names the commit it read at, and this guard now makes those counts checkable - but checkable is not the same as compliant, and the rule is the showcase record's to change.

Review's bottom line was that the status rule is near-vacuous - two sentences, one page, gated on the word 'marked' - and that the module could not detect the day a per-identifier status appeared. Both true. The answer is not a proximity reader: reading the pages is what showed why. Of the three places an identifier sits within forty characters of a status, two are the set claims and the third is a HALT CONDITION on phases/p1.html - 'ADR-013 or ADR-017 is still BLOCKED_BY_S01 or DRAFT_REQUIRED' - a disjunction over two ADRs and two statuses that asserts neither. With the entry criterion on phases/p0.html, the pattern is that this site states statuses mostly in CONDITIONALS, and a reader taking proximity for assertion would manufacture claims from both. So every reading is enumerated and classified by hand, and a fourth fails until a person says which kind it is.

A count in the docstring was false: it said every one of a hundred and ninety citations had a register row while the reader examined a hundred and eighty-one, because citations were read from the tag-stripped prose and nine live only inside an href. Citations now come from the source and claims from the prose, which is the right split - a citation is a mention, a claim is a sentence. Two published counts wrong in two consecutive packages, both from a reader I did not measure against the raw corpus.

Three further evasions were real and are closed: a set claim written 'flagged' rather than 'marked'; an identifier run longer than twelve chunks, which truncated silently and hid a genuine disagreement; and a count written in digits.
decisions: DEC-109: a sibling module, three rules, no content change.
assumptions: A status word in the register's own case, near a number or an identifier set, is a claim about the register; the same word in lowercase is ordinary English.
An entry criterion states a required future state and is not a claim about the present.

authority.page_content_change: NOT_GRANTED: #313 says a disagreement is reported before it is repaired, and none was found

stop_if: A page is edited to satisfy the guard before it is established whether the page or the register is the wrong one.
The count reader is widened to lowercase status words; it would read ordinary English as a claim.

declared_non_coverage: Prose paraphrases of a count are not read - 'Fourteen require a draft', 'Six wait on the first slice' - though both sit beside the numeric claims that are read, on the same page, and both are true.
Tags are stripped before reading, so the reader cannot tell a heading from a caption, nor which element a claim sits in.
It checks what a page says against the register; it does not check that the register is right.
An entry criterion's required future state is deliberately not read as a claim.
Telling an assertion from a condition is not attempted by the reader. Every status reading is classified by hand and a new one fails until someone classifies it.
An ADR cited inside an HTML comment is read as a citation, since citations come from the source; that is deliberate, because a commented-out citation still names an ADR.
